Without that, undo resurrects rows other devices deleted. An undo snapshot taken before the deletion still contains the entity, so restoring it records an
upsert
— which flushes as a
creation
and re-seeds every peer that had already agreed the row was gone. Undo is scoped to what the local user did; a deletion made on another device isn’t that.
An ID leaves the set as soon as it becomes local again — an explicit
, or storage handing the row back on a later merge — so a row that another device deletes and then restores is undoable once more. The set survives
, because a flush ends a pending write’s life, not a deletion’s.
